### D-720 — An implementation module lives in a folder the loader does not scan

> _2026-10-31 · core/blong-gogo · active_

adapter/server is not a directory of related modules but a list of base adapters and the handler
group each one serves: the loader scans it and imports every code file in every process that carries
the adapter realm, which is all of them, so a module without a default export is imported and
dropped — cost without registration — and a module with one becomes a child. The engine kinds and
the shared helpers therefore live elsewhere: src/agent/ for the kinds, reached only through the
computed await import in adapter/server/engine.ts, and src/adapter/impl/ for the helpers an adapter
imports (acl, pathRefresh, slackManifest, ngrokTunnels, workspaceFs, workspacePath).
folderShape.test.ts pins the folder to adapter instances and to group folders named after the base
that serves them, with no exceptions — the inbound half of slack and viber moved into slack/ and
viber/ for that reason, and the agent base became engine so its folder had a module of the same
name. The scan itself is load-bearing and was kept: removing children: `['./server']` and resolving
extends by convention made every extended instance lose its methods, because a base's handler groups
are children of the adapter realm and that is what registers them — the failing call was
workspace.repo.prepare not found. A lazy base would therefore have to load its groups with it
(T-593). The rule that stands: a heavy package is imported inside the function that needs it
(D-700), and anything that is not an instance belongs in a folder nothing scans.

### D-722 — A prototype is not a port: thunks live in their own map

> _2026-10-31 · core/blong-gogo · active_

Registry.start walks the ports, so registering a lazy base in ports does not defer it — it starts
it. The first attempt did exactly that and every base started, then kafka threw on a config section
the base never gets as a port. A prototype therefore needs a second map: registry.thunks holds a
resolver per name, start ignores it, createPort does not reach it, and AdapterBase's extends
resolution asks ports first and thunks second. The resolver registers the base's handler group as
methods — those are the base's methods, and an instance imports them — but never registers the
module as a layer, because a layer becomes a port. The realm declares thunk: `['./server']` instead
of children, and because every group folder is now named after its base the resolver needs no
manifest: each base module pairs with the group folder of the same name

### D-723 — kind drives the loop, provider says what the model speaks

> _2026-11-01 · core/blong-gogo · active_

An account now answers two questions instead of one. kind says who owns the loop (sim, vercel,
mastra, deepseek); provider says what wire format the model answers in, defaulting to the OpenAI
chat-completions shape because that is what services publish as their compatible endpoint — OpenAI,
Azure, Ollama, vLLM, LM Studio, OpenRouter, Groq, Together, Mistral, DeepSeek, xAI, Gemini's
compatibility base and Anthropic's own compatibility layer. Anthropic and gateway are native
providers, and both ship with the framework (@ai-sdk/anthropic and @ai-sdk/gateway beside ai); they
are still loaded through a computed specifier, so an image that prunes one starts and only the
account that names the missing one fails — the rule loadKind already follows. Base URL, key, headers
and the model name are the whole configuration, which is what stops a vendor from entering the code:
the two step engines now call one factory instead of building createOpenAI themselves. Reasoning
effort reaches the SDK as its own reasoning setting, which translates per provider rather than one
vendor's flag the rest ignore, and a parameters bag is merged last for the settings the typed fields
do not cover — so the escape hatch wins over the shortcut it overlaps.

### D-730 — blong-gogo: a model's Markdown becomes mrkdwn in the Slack port

> _2026-11-01 · core/blong-gogo · active_

A model answers in Markdown and Slack reads a dialect of it, so the answer was arriving as literal
punctuation. The translation lives in the slack adapter (adapter/server/slack/markdown.ts) and is
applied by slack.message.sendRequestSend, not in blong-chat or blong-agent: every platform has its
own dialect, so the realm must keep handing a port plain Markdown and the port owns what its
platform can read. Conversion and splitting are two functions on purpose, because a caller that
chunks text it already converted must not convert it a second time, where bold would turn into
italic. A table becomes a fenced block, the only shape a grid survives in a text message, and an
image becomes a link, because a text message cannot carry one.

### D-742 — The generic find normalises the order clause it is sent

> _2026-11-03 · core/blong-gogo · active_

The generic `find` in `core/blong-gogo/src/adapter/server/knex.ts` normalises the caller's order
clause before it reaches knex, and the `switch` fallthrough that throws `knex.generic` now warns
with the verb it did not recognise.

The normalisation is not cosmetic. A portal sends `orderBy: [{field, dir}]` (`useTableList`, the
Explorer) while knex reads `{column, order}`, and knex formats a term it cannot read as the
identifier `undefined`: the clause becomes an ordering by that name, and MySQL answers
`Unknown column 'undefined' in 'order clause'` on every column the reader sorts by. The shape had no
test because nothing sorts by default, so the defect appeared only when a reader clicked a header.
Both spellings are accepted rather than changing the client, because `{field, dir}` is what the
model system already documents and a browser is the harder thing to redeploy.

The warn is the part that matters for the next investigation. `knex.generic` is the one throw a
reader cannot attribute from the error: it names no verb, carries no SQL, and is a _declared_ error,
so the logging boundary treats it as expected and records nothing. That is why the marine family
tree was attributed to the reserved word `order` (T-599) when the report never said what was
actually wrong. A real driver failure carries its SQL; this throw carries a mystery, so it states
the verb and the method it could not serve.

Knex was never the suspect: it backticks every identifier the builder passes as an identifier, so a
sort on the reserved word reaches MySQL as an ordering by the backticked column.

### D-785 — Dates are normalised in the adapter, not left to the schema codec

> _2026-11-06 · core/blong-gogo · active_

The knex adapter normalises a date value at the database boundary: it discovers the date, datetime
and timestamp columns from INFORMATION_SCHEMA next to the binary(16) map, and rewrites an ISO
instant into the literal MySQL stores, the calendar day for a date column and UTC without a zone for
a datetime. The TypeBox codecs would do this on a typed schema, but a handler that overrides its
validation with a permissive payload (the flat profile of an athlete, the derived recipientKind of a
conferral) hands the string straight to knex, and MySQL refuses 2015-01-01T00:00:00.000Z with
Incorrect datetime value. A raw knex write in a realm does not pass through the adapter either,
which is why realm/blong-sport normalises the same way in profile.ts.

### D-803 — An encrypted body on a route that does not decode MLE is refused

> _2026-11-10 · core/blong-gogo · active_

The MLE hook runs on every gateway route and decodes params only where the route requires auth and
does not declare `mle: false`. It used to leave an encrypted body untouched everywhere else, and the
cast that followed turned it into the params object the schema wanted: the handler then reported
every required property as missing for a payload that carried all of them, which reads as a caller
bug and is a route decision. The hook now refuses such a body with `gateway.mleUndecoded` and a 400,
naming the method, the path, the cause and both fixes — send plain JSON, or require auth on the
route. The wording lives in `mleUndecoded` and the decision in `routeDecodesMle` and
`looksMleEncrypted`, all three exported so a test reads them without a gateway and a key pair. The
error is declared in `mle.ts` rather than the gateway's `errorMap` because this plugin never
receives the gateway's error factory, and its config is the gateway's own (`@@F-710`).

### D-816 — a local run names its own database

> _2026-11-11 · core/blong-gogo · active_

The choice is that a local run names its own database, and the framework load refuses anything else
before an adapter connects. Outside a release or an upgrade intent the srv.db connection must name a
loopback host and the database the dev intent derives from suite and user, and a block that names
anything else fails the load with the key, the value and the rc files the load read.

The reasoning the code will not show is about where a rule of this kind can live at all. The realm
cannot police it, because the rows were written through the shared srv.db port that no realm owns.
The dev CLI cannot be the only place either, because the accident came from a plain local start as
much as from the tap suite, and a rule that lives in one command is a rule the next command forgets.
What made the incident expensive was silence rather than the write itself: the run provisioned its
test accounts, the seed succeeded, and the only signal was a row that should not exist.

The alternative of documenting the rule in the rc template was rejected as the only measure. A
comment is not a check, and the file that caused the incident was a copy of a template with a block
filled in. The alternative of refusing every non-loopback connection without an exception was
rejected because a developer with a database in a container or a cluster would switch the guard off
entirely, which is worse than the accident. One opt-out key, allowRemote, written next to the reason
it is used, keeps the exception in the file somebody reads.

The cost accepted is a copy of the dev naming template inside the guard. A test asserts the copy
against the adapter's own template, so a change to one fails a test rather than a run, and the check
stays scoped to the srv block so that a realm's own adapter namespace and the remote database the
root rc reaches through db.sql are left alone.

### D-817 — a question can be a card in the message, not a dialog

> _2026-11-11 · core/blong-gogo · active_

A question can be a card in the message rather than a dialog. Slack's `block` container holds
`input` blocks and an actions block, so a radio group or a checkbox list and a text box sit in the
conversation itself and are submitted together; that is `presentation: 'inlineForm'`. The
alternative, `form`, opens a modal and hides the question from the channel it was asked in, which is
the wrong trade for a plan's question and the reason the inline surfaces are the ones the
instructions recommend.

The submitted payload is the same object a modal sends: `state.values[<block_id>][<action_id>]`,
with `selected_option` for a radio, `selected_options` for checkboxes and `value` for a text input.
One reader in the port therefore answers both surfaces, which is why the block ids in the card are
the modal's (`choice`, `values`, `text`). The container is available in messages and home tabs,
holds at most ten children, and its title is required and capped at 150 characters.

The difference from a modal is enforcement. Slack validates an input block in a modal —
`optional: false` is a rule — and validates nothing in a message, so a Submit with every field empty
settles the question with only the sender. A caller that needs an answer has to read the answer and
ask again; a prompt is a question, not a form submission.

The work is three files: the presentation vocabulary in `core/blong/chat.ts`, the card in
`core/blong-gogo/src/adapter/server/slack/blocks.ts`, and the state reader in `slackInMessage.ts`,
which gained the typed text beside the selections. Both live proofs came from a real workspace: a
radio card answered `value: dev`, a text card answered its sentence, and a card submitted empty
answered with nothing but the sender.

### D-818 — a question defaults to the card in the message

> _2026-11-11 · core/blong-gogo · active_

A question's default presentation is the card in the message (`inlineForm`), not a dialog and not
the point-free inline form. A caller that says nothing gets the surface that keeps the question
where it was asked and accepts typing beside the options; naming `inline` or `form` is an override
for a question that wants buttons only, or a dialog of several answers.

Two cases are not the caller's to carry. A confirmation stays plain inline, because two buttons need
no card around them and a card would be decoration. And a card whose children would exceed the ten
blocks the platform allows is not posted broken and not refused: the port falls back to the dialog
when the question takes typing, and to the plain inline controls when it does not — so a question
that outgrows the card still asks, and a caller never has to compute the platform's limit.

The default lives in the port rather than in the caller because it is a rendering choice: the same
`chat.prompt.ask` should look right on Slack without every caller repeating `presentation`. The
trade-off is that a change of default changes every caller's surface at once, which is why the
fallback is a rule rather than an error and why the layers below the default stay reachable by name.

### D-819 — A long list is a dropdown, not a dialog

> _2026-11-11 · core/blong-gogo · active_

A list longer than ten options cannot be a radio group or a checkbox list anywhere in Slack — a
card, a dialog and a plain actions block all refuse the eleventh — so the over-ten case is not what
the child-block fallback was written for: that fallback stays for a card that genuinely cannot be
built, and it has not fired since the card holds at most three children. The long list is answered
where it was asked, with a static_select for a choice and a multi_static_select for a multiple
choice, which take a hundred options and report selected_option and selected_options exactly as the
radios do, so one reader in the port still turns every surface into the same answer. A dialog for a
long list would be a second surface for no gain, and the reason the card is the default is that the
question should not leave the conversation.

### D-821 — The port subscribes the message events it reads

> _2026-11-11 · core/blong-gogo · active_

The scope alone changed nothing: the app's manifest showed bot_events as message.channels and
message.im, so a private channel's message was never posted to the hook, and a typed reply could not
answer a question asked in a plan channel. A scope is permission to read a conversation; an event
subscription is Slack deciding to tell you about it, and the two are separate settings. The port
already rewrites the manifest at ready to point both request URLs at its address, so it now
subscribes the three message events it reads in the same pass and treats a manifest missing one as
out of date — otherwise a deployment would sit on the old subscription until someone remembered.
Events are added, never replaced, so a realm that listens to something else keeps it.

### D-828 — An order term the table cannot resolve is dropped, not fatal

> _2026-11-12 · core/blong-gogo · active_

The generic find used to turn a caller's order clause straight into the statement, so a term naming
something the table does not have failed the whole read. The ACL browse page hit it with
`targetName`: a browser model's display field, joined in from `core_resource` for reading and never
stored on the row, which MySQL rejects with `Unknown column 'targetName' in 'order clause'` — and
the page showed an error dialog instead of its fifteen rules.

The rule is now that an order term the read cannot resolve is dropped and logged, never fatal. Order
is presentation; no row is worth losing over it. A dotted name and a label alias are kept because
the read knows how to reach them, and everything else has to be a declared property of the object.
The browser cannot know a table's columns — it derives the default order from a model's name field,
which may be computed — so the side that holds the schema is the side that decides, and it decides
silently enough to keep the page usable and loudly enough (a warning naming the column) to find the
model that asked.

The opposite rule holds for filters: a `where` term on a missing column still fails, because
ignoring a filter shows rows the reader asked not to see, while ignoring an order only changes their
sequence.

### D-850 — An unknown-length stream reaches S3 through the SDK's uploader

> _2026-11-14 · core/blong-gogo · active_

An object store signs a `PutObject` request's length before the first byte exists, so the SDK
refuses a stream of unknown length ("Invalid value undefined for header
x-amz-decoded-content-length") and the server answers `MissingContentLength` when the chunked form
is turned off. The blob realm encrypts while it reads, so it cannot know the ciphertext length up
front, and buffering a 200 MiB upload would undo the design.
`core/blong-gogo/src/adapter/server/s3.ts` therefore keeps `PutObjectCommand` for a body whose
length is known — a buffer, a local file, a `fetch` with a `content-length` — and hands an
unknown-length stream to `@aws-sdk/lib-storage`'s `Upload`, which parts and signs the request as it
goes. That is a framework change, not a realm one, because every realm that streams to a bucket
meets the same wall; the dependency (`@aws-sdk/lib-storage`) sits beside the client it wraps.

### D-858 — A bare positional is an intent; a target is spelled as a path

> _2026-11-14 · core/blong-gogo · active_

A target used to be whichever positional named something that existed on disk. That made the meaning
of an argument depend on the working directory: a realm whose blob store lives in `dev/blob`
(`@@D-845`) grows a folder called `dev`, and `blong dev` then resolved to _that folder_ — the loader
imported a directory and failed with `ERR_UNSUPPORTED_DIR_IMPORT` while the command read as the
`dev` intent (`@@T-687`). So the discriminator is the argument's shape, not the filesystem: a
positional carrying a separator (`./dev`, `dev/`, `/opt/deploy/suite`) may name a target, and a bare
word is always an intent. The `exists` check stays, but only to confirm a path that was already
spelled as one — a path that is not there is still reported by the loader rather than silently read
as an intent.

Two things follow. A person who means the folder writes `./dev`, which is how a shell has always
asked for one, and `blong realm dev` scaffolds a realm called `dev` even inside a folder that holds
one, because the guard that keeps `realm` from being a command reads the same rule. The rule lives
in `core/blong-gogo/src/cliTarget.ts` and both binaries call it, so `blong` and `blong-watch` cannot
drift; its test pins each shape, including the one that cost a debugging session — `dev` beside a
`dev/` directory.

### D-860 — A stream body is the route's request, not the process's

> _2026-11-15 · core/blong-gogo · active_

`rawBody` used to be a property of the process: the gateway registered a `'*'` content type parser
on its own instance, so every route of every suite began accepting bodies no parser understood — a
JSON route that received `image/png` got a stream where it expected an object. It was also
unreachable from a realm: a child realm's config keys are its own block, so a companion that serves
files could not switch it on and every host had to repeat the line (`@@D-841`).

So the flag moved to the route, and then the process-wide form was deleted rather than deprecated.
`blob.upload.write` declares `rawBody: true`, the gateway carries it into the fastify route config,
and the routes that ask for it are mounted inside an encapsulated context that owns the parser.
Fastify's parsers are encapsulated like hooks — a child instance's parser reaches that instance's
routes and no others — so the upload route takes the bytes while every other route of the same
process still answers `415` for a content type it cannot read. Two forms of one switch is one form
too many: a suite that set `gateway.rawBody` asked for every route to accept anything, which is a
thing no suite should be able to say by accident, and leaving it in place would have kept the wrong
default reachable.

The rule is pinned in `core/blong-gogo/src/rawBody.test.ts`: one route in a child context takes
`image/png`, and the route beside it on the parent still refuses it. That is fastify's promise
rather than ours, and the gateway's mounting depends on it, so it is asserted where it can break.

### D-896 — The vocabulary lives in a `lukaot` layer of its own

> _2026-11-18 · core/blong-gogo · active_

Planned in `plans/lukaot/plan.md`.

A layer named for the

package, holding `lukaot/error.ts` and `lukaot/signal.ts`, is where a reader looks for the signals a
realm may emit — not a file called `error` that also declares logs. It costs a `WELL_KNOWN_LAYERS`
entry carrying the `error` layer's activation, a loader case, a kukum primitive and a
conventions-table row, which is the price of a name that does not lie. `error/` keeps loading as a
legacy source of error signals until each realm is converted.

### D-904 — A level call that dumps a payload is not a signal, and stays one

> _2026-11-18 · core/blong-gogo · active_

The plan says the framework's 93 level calls become declared signals, and 40 of them cannot: they
pass a **payload**, not a sentence. The shapes are `this.log?.trace(request)`,
`this.log?.trace({headers, body, statusCode})`, `this.log?.warn?.(error)` with an Error object, and
`this.log?.info?.('${METHOD} ${url}')` built from parts. A declaration's message is a string with
`{placeholders}`, and rendering an object into one produces `[object Object]` — the reason these
calls take a structured first argument at all is that the reader wants the structure.

So the boundary is drawn by shape, not by count: a site whose argument is a sentence (a string
literal or `{message: '…', …fields}`) converts, and its extra fields become the signal's `params`; a
site that dumps a payload or an Error stays a level call, because converting it would silently
replace structured output with a string.

What changes for a converted site with extra fields is nesting: `{workspace, accounts, message}`
used to spread its fields at the top of the record, and they now travel under `params`. That is the
convergence working as intended — one place for a signal's values — but it is a visible change in
JSON output and should be stated rather than discovered.

The count, measured rather than assumed: of the 108 original sites, 31 are sentence-shaped and 40
are payload-shaped (the rest are mentions in prose and comments). 36 are converted as of this note.

### D-905 — The logging facade and the emitter move in one step

> _2026-11-19 · core/blong-gogo · active_

`semanticContext.ts` is renamed `responseContext.ts` and every importer follows, but its imports —
and those of `checkpoint.ts`, `Registry.ts`, `AdapterBase.ts` and `Gateway.ts` — still come from
`@feasibleone/semantic-log` (`/attachable`, `/capability`). The re-point to `@feasibleone/lukaot`
rides with the emitter swap (T-715) instead.

The reason is that `AsyncLocalStorage` is per package: `core/semantic-log/src/context.ts` and
`core/lukaot/src/context.ts` each construct their own instance, and the facade (`/attachable`'s
`vocabulary`) delegates to whichever storage its own package owns. An identity bound through
lukaot's facade would therefore be invisible to every record the old emitter writes: the flow, the
leg and the trace would simply be absent from the output, with no error to notice — the failure mode
@@F-763 describes, where a converted site silently stopped carrying context.

`Gateway.ts`'s `TRACE_HEADER` and `withoutCapabilities` cannot move on their own either: both live
in `propagation.ts`, which imports `./context.ts`, so the root entry pulls `node:async_hooks` into
whatever graph imports it, and the bundle-safe subpath (`@feasibleone/lukaot/context`) re-exports
only `attachable.ts` and cannot reach them without a cycle.

So the unit of change is "the facade and the emitter", not "the file that reads them". T-713 keeps
the part that is independent — the name — and T-715 takes the rest.

### D-907 — AdapterBase.error keeps its line until errors declare themselves

> _2026-11-19 · core/blong-gogo · active_

`AdapterBase.error()` keeps its log line. The original task removed it on the grounds that "an error
has recorded itself when it was constructed", and that is true of a lukaot **error signal** —
`createErrorEmitter` writes the record and hands back the failure to throw (D-890) — but not of an
`ITypedError` from the framework's own error factory, which records nothing until something writes
it.

The de-logging waits for the error factory itself to become a declared vocabulary, where the
identifier that names the case is the same call that records it. Until then the method keeps what it
does — stamp `$meta.method`, answer `$meta.expect` at debug, otherwise write at error.

What it writes changed once the emitter was lukaot's, and the shape is worth stating because the
first version was wrong in a way only a record dump showed. It used to hand the error as the
_fields bag_ — `log.error?.(error)` — and `Error`'s `message` and `stack` are not enumerable, so the
record carried `msg: ""` and no stack at all: only the enumerable extras (`type`, `statusCode`,
`params`, `method`) by the time the fields were copied. Under pino that lost the same two things;
nothing had noticed because the line still appeared. It now writes
`{$meta: {mtid: 'error', method}, err: error, type, statusCode, params, validation}` with
`error.message` as the sentence, so the record has the message, the stack in lukaot's error slot,
`operation` on the header, and the values as fields.

What is still missing is the _identity_: an `ITypedError` carries `type` but no declared identifier,
so an operator cannot raise or silence one case. That is the same follow-up as the de-logging, not a
separate one.

### D-908 — A realm owns its vocabulary, not the layer that declares it

> _2026-11-19 · core/blong-gogo · active_

A realm declares its vocabulary once, in `lukaot/error.ts` and `lukaot/signal.ts`, and it is the
realm's rather than the folder's. The first version pushed the declaration onto the result of the
layer that declared it, which worked only while the declaring file lived in a layer that also had a
port — an `error/error.ts` beside the handlers it served. A `lukaot/` folder has no port and no
methods, so nothing was attached: `port.signal` was undefined in every handler, every
`port.signal?.x?.()` was a silent no-op, and the only thing that noticed was a test that read the
store afterwards.

The realm now owns one array and points every layer's result at it, so a declaration loaded after a
port was assembled is still in the array when the port attaches, and every handler in the realm
reads the same proxy. The alternative — declaring the vocabulary inside each layer that uses it —
would have made the same names appear once per layer and drift, which is the thing a declaration
exists to prevent.

A layer with no port no longer tries to attach at all; it contributes to the array and stops.

### D-909 — The framework log promotes the declared identifier onto the record the service reads

> _2026-11-19 · core/blong-gogo · active_

The framework's log writes a signal's declared identifier as a _field_, because that is where
lukaot's printer reads it to print `signal: frameworkWatchFileChanged` beneath the line. The
service's sink counts a record by its top-level identity and drops any record that names none. Both
are right about their own half, and the two had never met: every record this framework wrote was
dropped before it left the process, so the service's templates, flows, diagrams, search and digest
were empty in every run and nothing failed.

The promotion is done in the adapter that joins the two, `LukaotLog`'s single write path, rather
than by loosening the sink. Teaching the sink to read an identity out of arbitrary fields would let
any record with a `signal` field masquerade as a declared signal, which is exactly the distinction
the service's ledger is built on. The adapter is the one place that knows both that the field came
from a declaration and that the record is on its way to the service.

### D-920 — The browser platform attaches the vocabulary, and a page reads it through its log

> _2026-11-19 · core/blong-gogo · active_

The browser platform attaches the declared vocabulary like the server does, and a page's component
reaches one through its log. Two halves, each fixing a different kind of silence. The loader no
longer resolves the attacher to nothing for the browser, so a browser handler's `this.signal` is the
layer's proxy exactly as on the server; the skip existed because `signals.ts` reached lukaot's root,
which reached pino and `node:async_hooks`, and the root has been platform-free since the node half
moved behind `@feasibleone/lukaot/node` (`@@D-912`). `BrowserLog` gains `signalFor(name, level)`
over the vocabularies the packages in the process contributed, because a page has no port for the
realms it does not own and a component extending `Internal` reads its proxy from the log.

The realm's own names are contributed rather than only declared, since `contributedVocabularies()`
is what `signalFor` composes and what every port's attacher composes first (`@@D-918`); one file in
`core/blong-browser/lukaot/` therefore reaches both a handler and a component, and `browser.ts`
globs the folder so it is loaded at all.

What keeps this honest is `core/blong-browser/src/browserBundle.test.ts`: it builds the browser
variant and fails on a node builtin or a server-only module appearing in the graph, which is the
check that a page still cannot reach the server runtime. It passes with the attacher enabled, which
is the evidence the skip is no longer needed.

### D-923 — A capture's enabled is the configuration's call, read once at construction

> _2026-11-20 · core/blong-gogo · active_

A capture's `enabled` is the configuration's decision, and the declaration's is only the default it
starts from. Three states, read in that order: an `enabled` in the process's `log.capture.<id>`
block wins; a block that names the capture without saying either way means run, because naming it is
the ask; and with no block at all the declaration's own flag decides, so the framework can ship its
three captures off while a realm that needs one declares it on. This is the same order a log
signal's policy resolves in, and it exists because the opposite — the declaration as the last word —
made an operator's `enabled: true` unreachable (@@F-770).

The policy is read once, when the log is built. Not lazily, and not per call: the configuration the
loader hands over is the runtime's live proxy, whose factory-phase guard turns a leaf read during a
handler factory into a thrown error, and a capture has no way to know whether a factory is running
when a payload arrives (@@F-771). Copying the block puts capture rungs in the same class as `level`,
`format` and `redact` — settings fixed for the life of the process — so a change takes effect on the
next start. If capture rungs ever need to follow a config reload, the way to do it is a
version-checked snapshot, not a live read at the call site.

What is deliberately not decided here: the payload thunk still decides whether the shape is
rendered, and `sample` still thins calls after the policy says yes. `enabled` answers only "may this
capture run at all".

### D-924 — A capture is scoped by its adapter instance, matched on the port id

> _2026-11-20 · core/blong-gogo · active_

A capture is scoped by a `when` block whose first identity is the **adapter instance**:
`instance: [srv.http]`, matched against the id the framework assembles the port with,
`<realm>.<layer>`. That id is the grain the capture requirement asks for — "a deployment turns
capture on for the one adapter it is debugging, and the other instances of the same adapter pay
nothing" — and it was missing: the shipped selector matched `method` and `phase` only, so two
instances of one adapter could not be told apart and the requirement's own example
(`when: {instance: [subjectHttp]}`) had nothing to match. The instance is already the record's
`context` and already reaches `captureFor(name)`, so nothing new is plumbed and the surface is still
built per port; `LukaotLog.#resolveCapture` simply receives the name it was called with.

The selector is where per-instance configuration lives, rather than a `capture` block inside each
adapter's own config: the loader judges unknown keys per module against an allow-list built from the
module's structure and its source config blocks, so a `capture` key in every adapter block is a
change to every adapter, while a selector on the one `log.capture` block needs nothing. Because
every field is a glob, the same mechanism covers the coarser grains the requirement listed —
`srv.*` is one realm's adapters, `*.http` is the http adapter wherever it runs — without inventing
separate `adapter` and `realm` keys whose values would have to be derived from the same id.

What the selector does not do is beat the declaration's own `enabled`: the three framework captures
ship off, so an instance-scoped policy must still say `enabled: true` (or name the capture, which is
the ask). That is deliberate — the selector narrows _where_, the flag decides _whether_ (`@@F-770`).

### D-925 — A capture's when block may key one rule per instance

> _2026-11-20 · core/blong-gogo · active_

`when` accepts a key per instance beside the flat fields. Each key is an instance id (a glob works)
and its value is that instance's whole rule: `true` captures everything it does, `false` captures
nothing, and an object narrows `method`/`phase` and may raise `level` or add a `mask`. Listing
instances is what makes the list the rule — an instance that matches none of the keys takes no
capture — because the alternative reading, "keys are overrides and the rest follow the policy",
makes `when: {srv.http: true}` capture everywhere, which is the opposite of what writing one key
means. `'*'` is how a configuration says "everything else".

The most specific key wins: a literal id before a glob, a longer glob before a shorter one, so
`srv.http` beats `srv.*` beats `*`. The rules are ordered once, when the policy is copied at
construction, so the resolver's first match is the answer and a call pays no comparison. A rule's
`level` and `mask` override the policy's for that instance and nothing else, which is what makes
"one adapter at `body`, the rest at `line`" a single block rather than two captures.

The flat `instance`/`method`/`phase` fields stay as the shorthand for the single-instance case and
are not consulted when keys are present, so a block never says two things at once. `sample` stays
policy-level: it thins every instance the same way, and a per-instance draw rate would make the
count of records depend on which adapter happened to be busiest.

### D-929 — A destination is named by configuration, not by a dependency

> _2026-11-20 · core/blong-gogo · active_

The framework must not name `tools/blong-log`: a realm or a suite that wants its records in a viewer
may not exist in a deployment that installs the viewer, and `core/blong-gogo` cannot depend on a
tool. So the wiring is named by configuration instead. A `log.destination` block carries `module`
and `options`, the loader imports that module and calls its default export with the options, and
what comes back must be a lukaot `Writer` — the same object `setWriter` takes, so a test's own
module is as valid as the shipped one. `destination: '<module>'` is the shorthand with no options.

The name is resolved from the working directory the configuration was read from, not from the file
that imports it — otherwise a bare package name would never resolve, since the importing package is
precisely the one that does not depend on it. An absolute path, a `file:` URL and a relative path
are honoured so a test can name its own fixture.

Every failure — the module will not import, exports no factory, throws while starting, or answers no
writer — is reported through the log the seam sits beside and then skipped. A wrong viewer address
costs the records it would have received, never the process that was writing them; throwing at boot
would make a mistyped port a worse outcome than no viewer. A destination that does load is closed
with the process, `close()` then `flush()`, because the last batch would otherwise be lost in a
socket's queue.

### D-931 — The framework states the intent at the outermost entry

> _2026-11-20 · core/blong-gogo · active_

`intent` answers who asked and for what, and the only place that knows both halves is the outermost
entry: the method the request was addressed to is what the work is for, and an authorised request
names its actor (`$meta.auth.actorId`). So `runInFlow` states it once — `{name: kind, actor}` — and
every record the request produces carries it without a realm inventing a spelling.

It is set in `runInFlow` rather than at a call site because that is the one function that knows the
entry is outermost: a nested leg would otherwise restate its own method as the reason the whole
request exists, and the record would name the hop instead of the purpose. A realm that has a better
answer calls `withIntent` inside the request, which overrides this for everything it covers — the
ambient scope keeps the nearest declaration.

Absent rather than half-filled: an unlabelled flow has no intent worth recording, and a request that
was never authorised has no actor, so neither is invented. `withIntent` reached the framework
through the attached vocabulary rather than an import, the way the rest of the emitter's scope does,
because this file is also loaded by the browser bootstrap (`@@D-905`).

### D-941 — Call recording is switched at runtime, not only at load

> _2026-11-20 · core/blong-gogo · active_

Call recording has three grains, and each answers a different question. One flow decides through the
calls capability, published with the execution: a grant header turns it on for one request, and a
flow already running keeps the answer it entered with, which is why a switch never changes a call
half way through. The process decides through log.calls, and at start-up that is enough.

The third grain is the one this entry is about: the process has to be able to change its mind while
it runs. A value that can only change at start-up is a value an operator cannot use on the process
that is misbehaving - and here the value decides whether the flow ledger, and so every flow page and
every diagram, sees anything at all. So Log.calls is re-applied on a config reload, and the log
component is asked directly by the reload pipeline (applyConfigReload), because it is not a port and
nothing in the port pass would ever reach it. Registry exposes it as logComponent; the name is not
log because Internal already owns that member.

setCallRecording is the imperative half, and deliberately the only one: it patches callTrace.ts's
module configuration, so a source that is not configuration - an operator's endpoint now, a value a
deployment keeps in its database later - calls it once and nothing else in the package learns about
that source. The patch replaces off rather than merging it, because a list that merged could never
lose an entry.

The switch reports itself as frameworkCallRecordingChanged. A quiet flow ledger has to be legible as
a decision: the alternative is an operator looking for a defect in a deployment that was told to
stop recording, which is the same class of confusion the empty pages caused when the call channel
silently produced nothing at all.

### D-945 — A capture policy is switched by replacing the snapshot the resolver reads

> _2026-11-20 · core/blong-gogo · active_

The call switch moved into a running process (D-941), and the capture policies were left behind:
they were snapshotted when the log component was constructed, and the note on the follow-up assumed
the capture view a port holds embeds that snapshot. It does not. A surface is built from the
declared captures and a resolve callback, and the callback asks the log for the policy on every
capture — so making the snapshot replaceable was the whole fix, and no port had to be rebuilt, which
is what the reload pipeline could not have done anyway: a log-only config change marks no port
affected.

setCapture replaces the snapshot and the resolver reads it; configChanged re-applies log.capture
beside log.calls, because a component that is not a port is asked once per reload and has to answer
for both. frameworkCaptureChanged reports the switch for the same reason
frameworkCallRecordingChanged does: a capture an operator turned on and sees nothing from must be
confirmed from the log, and one turned off must not read later as a broken adapter.

One thing stays as it was: a policy can only switch a capture some source declares, so a
configuration naming an identifier nobody declares records nothing. That is not a gap but the
declaration being the closed set.

### D-948 — A subscription is a realm method; a frame carries a cursor

> _2026-11-21 · core/blong-gogo · active_

A subscription is a method of a realm, not a transport a realm opens. A route declares
`stream: true` (or `{heartbeatMs}`) beside `rawBody`/`bundle`, its handler answers an async
iterable, and the gateway writes one server-sent event per yielded value on the same route,
authorized by the same capability and traced as the same flow. The realm never imports `ws`, never
sees a socket and never checks a token. Implemented as `core/blong-gogo/src/gatewayStream.ts`
(frames, heartbeat, backpressure, abort, one `error` event) with the gateway's `_serveStream`
keeping the flow open for the stream's life and `$meta.abort` aborting when the reader leaves; the
realm's `viewer.entry.watch` wakes a reader with `{last, size}`.

The rule the design turns on: **a frame carries a cursor, never a record.** A response that arrives
as a sequence has no single body for the gateway to sign and encrypt, so a frame is protected by the
connection and the caller's authorization only — the per-response MLE envelope every other answer
gets does not apply. A wake fits under that ceiling (a ULID names nothing on its own) and the
records keep travelling over the ordinary encrypted `viewer.entry.find`, which is also why the wake
follows `realm/blong-agent/adapter/notify.ts`: a wake is a nudge, not a transport (`@@D-709`).

The page still polls. Its transport is the browser's codec stack (`adapter.http` extended as
`backend`, with `codec.mle`), whose `exec` resolves a whole body and whose MLE decrypts one response
object — so a browser cannot yet consume a stream, and giving it one is a separate change in the
most sensitive part of that stack. What landed is the server half plus a wake no page uses yet; the
client half, and how a page is told to use it, is still open.

### D-949 — A stream is a realm generator; sealing is the route's call

> _2026-11-21 · core/blong-gogo · active_

The transport decisions the owner set, implemented in `core/blong-gogo/src/gatewayStream.ts`,
`Gateway.ts`, `mle.ts` and the two codecs, and in `core/blong-mle` (`streamCipher.ts`,
`streamFrame.ts`, `streamRead.ts`). The primitive is deliberately generic — values, envelopes and
frames, nothing about logs — because other routes will stream too.

A route streams when its handler answers an **async iterable** and the caller asked; the caller asks
with `$meta.stream`, which `codec.jsonrpc` turns into the `Accept` envelope (text for a person,
binary for a program), and an ordinary call is answered as JSON exactly as before. Sealing is the
route's decision and on by default, with `stream: {encrypt: false}` the opt-out and `stream: false`
a refusal; a caller cannot negotiate secrecy, since a readable envelope would be a downgrade. A
route with nothing secret to send opted out while the wake was the only stream; it now seals too,
because the sealed path is the one a browser exercises and an opt-out would leave it untested.

**One frame is not one value.** A writer may hold values and send them together, so a frame carries
`STREAM_FLAG_BATCH` and a JSON array when it does, and every consumer flattens. A handler that
yields an array still sends one value, because the flag — not the shape — says "batch". The readable
envelope keeps one value per event on purpose.

The cipher is the record model: HKDF(ECDH(server private encrypt key, client public encrypt key),
salt) with the salt in `x-blong-stream-salt`, AES-256-GCM per frame, nonce = 4 zero bytes + the
frame's sequence, `info` = `blong.stream.v1:<method>` from `streamInfoOf`. A fresh salt per stream
is what makes a zero nonce prefix safe. The key is agreed by the **MLE plugin's own crypto**
(`mle.streamKey`, reached through a request hook), not from the gateway's config, because that
config carries only the public JWK (D-441) — a stream that tried to agree from it had nothing to
agree with.

A frame is `[u32 length][u8 flags][payload]`, defined once in `streamFrame.ts` for both sides; a
sealed payload is `[u64 seq][ciphertext + tag]`, the sequence living there and nowhere else because
it is the nonce's tail. The length is the one field a peer controls, so `STREAM_MAX_FRAME_BYTES` (1
MiB) is enforced on both sides: a reader refuses an announced length above it on the prefix, before
accumulating anything, and a writer handed a larger frame ends the stream with one `error` frame.

The consumer half is `readStream`, which takes a response — a Fetch `ReadableStream` or a Node
stream, with either header shape — and yields values: both envelopes, the length cap, the batch flag
and the per-frame decryption. A reader that stops closes the response (`reader.cancel()`), so a page
that navigated away does not leave a producer running.

### D-950 — A stream frame carries a 1 MiB cap, enforced by writer and reader

> _2026-11-21 · core/blong-gogo · active_

A frame is `[u32 length][u8 flags][payload]`, and the length is the one field a peer controls before
anything else has been read. A reader that trusted it would allocate whatever the peer wrote there
and then wait for that many bytes — a number the peer need never send — so the cap is enforced on
both ends instead of being a convention. `STREAM_MAX_FRAME_BYTES` (1 MiB) lives in
`core/blong-mle/src/streamFrame.ts` beside the codec, because it is a property of the format and not
of whoever reads it.

The reader checks the announced length on the four-byte prefix, before accumulating a single byte of
payload: a length above the cap ends the stream with `stream.frameTooLarge` naming the limit and the
method. The writer checks the frame it built and, for one above the cap, sends a single `error`
frame and ends — so a producer's mistake reaches the producer's route and its caller, rather than
becoming a reader that refuses a prefix and a page that silently stops updating.

One megabyte rather than "whatever fits": it is far above any value a route streams today (a log
wake, a progress line) and far below a heap that would hurt, so a legitimate producer never meets
the limit and a hostile one cannot choose how much memory the reader holds. A route that genuinely
needs bigger values sends more frames; the cap is per frame, not per stream.

### D-955 — The binary envelope carries a keepalive frame

> _2026-11-21 · core/blong-gogo · active_

The binary envelope gets a keepalive frame: a frame with no payload and a new flag,
`STREAM_FLAG_KEEPALIVE`, which every reader skips (`valuesOfFrame` returns nothing for it).
`writeEventStream` writes one as soon as the stream opens and one on each idle tick where nothing
else was written, in place of the SSE comment the text envelope has always used.

Three things decided it. A reader of a quiet stream could not tell it from a dead one — the text
envelope has said "still here" every fifteen seconds since it existed, and the binary one said
nothing ever. Worse for a page, the response headers ride with the first byte of the body, so an
intermediary that holds a response until it has one kept a just-opened subscription invisible until
the first record arrived, which on a quiet process is never; that is what made the portal's log page
report its stream as closed while the server had opened it. And the reader that needs this most is
the binary one: a program with no person watching cannot fall back on noticing that the screen
stopped moving.

It is a flag rather than a length-zero frame because a zero-length frame is already a legitimate
value — the empty string — and the reader must not have to guess. It is never sealed, even on a
route that seals everything else: an empty frame carries nothing to protect, and sealing it would
spend a sequence number on nothing, making the reader pay for crypto to learn that nothing happened.
The sequence numbering therefore stays with the sealed frames alone, which is why a keepalive can be
written by an encoder that has no key.

The alternative was to leave the envelope alone and let the spec produce the record it waits for.
That would have fixed the test and left the product unable to answer the question a log tail exists
to answer — is this still live? — so it was rejected.

### D-956 — An empty answer is null, in both envelopes

> _2026-11-22 · core/blong-gogo · active_

A route that answers nothing answers `null`. A JSON-RPC response carries exactly one of `result` and
`error`, so `result: undefined` is not an empty answer but a missing one: `JSON.stringify` drops the
key and the client's codec refuses the body as `jsonrpcEmpty`, and the sealed envelope is worse
because the serializer does not drop anything — an empty schema, which is what a permissive `result`
compiles to, renders the four characters `undefined` into the payload, which is not JSON, so a
browser reports a parse error instead of the answer it received.

Both envelopes read one value, so both are fixed in one place: `gatewayAnswer.jsonRpcAnswer` builds
the body with `result` coerced by `?? null`, and the MLE hook applies the same rule for a route that
answers nothing on its own. `null` rather than a typed error because an empty answer is an answer —
a handler that forgot to return something is a contract the route declared in its schema, and
refusing it at the envelope would turn every such route into a 500.

The `??` is deliberate rather than `=== undefined`: a falsy result (`0`, `false`, the empty string)
is a value a caller asked for and must survive, which is the half a later "simplification" would
break.

### D-957 — A refused request is a typed 400 that names its fields

> _2026-11-22 · core/blong-gogo · active_

A request whose body, query or params does not match the schema its route declares is answered as a
typed 400, `gateway.validationFailed`, carrying `validation` as the list of `{field, message}` pairs
the browser's Editor paints beside its inputs. The type is what a run that probes a refusal on
purpose declares in `expect`, so the refusal is recorded at debug level instead of as an unhandled
error.

It used to be a plain `Error` from the TypeBox check, which reached four places as a defect: the
client was told "internal server error" for a payload it could have fixed, the process wrote an
unhandled-error record with a stack, an observer of the deployment counted a failing call that had
failed for the caller's own reason, and an expected-errors declaration had no type to name.

Two shapes decided it. The status is 400 rather than 500 because nothing about the process failed —
a caller's mistake is not the framework's. And the fields travel in `validation` rather than only in
the message because the sentence is for a person reading a log while the list is what a form can
use; the message still spells them out, so a grep and a reader both find the field that was wrong.

### D-958 — A repeated signal inside a grace window is the same Ctrl+C

> _2026-11-22 · core/blong-gogo · active_

The shutdown handler used to treat every signal after the first as an operator demanding a forced
exit, so one Ctrl+C printed "shutting down on SIGINT" immediately followed by "second SIGINT
received, forcing exit" and cut the cleanup short. A terminal signals the whole foreground group,
and a package manager forwards what it received to the process it started, which is in that same
group: one keystroke is delivered twice, milliseconds apart. Measured with two probe processes: a
parent that forwards SIGINT gives its child two deliveries from a single group signal.

The fix is a grace window (`repeatGraceMs`, 1000ms by default) rather than any inspection of the pid
or the process group, because the two deliveries are indistinguishable in what they carry. A
deliberate second press comes after the operator has waited, and the bounded `timeoutMs` still
covers a shutdown that hangs, so nothing is lost by ignoring a repeat inside the window. The cost of
finding this is recorded as F-812.

### D-959 — Runtime warnings are reported as records, not instead of stderr

> _2026-11-22 · core/blong-gogo · active_

Node raises deprecations, listener leaks and a log destination that refused a batch as `warning`
events, and those reached the terminal only: a served process's records never carried them. The
destination failure is the one that matters most, because its own record would travel in the very
batch that was refused (F-811).

Node prints the warning to stderr and calls the listener as well, so the record is an addition
rather than a replacement, and the diagnosis survives a broken destination. The guard against the
reporter hearing itself spans the whole event-loop turn, because `process.emitWarning` delivers on
`process.nextTick`: a sink that warns while its record is written is heard after that write
returned, so a flag cleared in `finally` guards nothing and the turn writes another record into the
same sink, a spin that never yields to I/O. `setImmediate` is the release point, and its handle is
unref'd. The consequence is that a second, unrelated warning arriving in the same turn is dropped; a
broken destination is separately bounded by the writer reporting each failure kind once, so one
warning cannot become a stream. Installed once per process, since a suite loads two platforms that
share one, and reachable only through `platform.logComponent`: `load()` answers the registry rather
than the api it built, which is why that accessor is now declared on IRegistry (F-813).

### D-961 — The schema generator reports what it writes, not what it scans

> _2026-11-22 · core/blong-gogo · active_

The generator has three jobs and only the last one is worth a line. A scan records which files an
orchestrator folder already holds; a `schema()` pass pairs a loaded API method with a folder whose
`<subject><object>` prefix matches and whose file is absent; the write fills an empty handler file
with the signature the API declares. The scan runs for every handler group of every realm, twice for
some folders in one load, and again on every reload, so announcing it announced folders that would
never generate anything and buried the line that mattered (F-814).

The rule now is that a report follows the effect: the scan writes nothing and reports nothing, and
`frameworkSchemaFileRewritten` is emitted at the one moment a stub is written. Three defects were
fixed along the way, each of which made the old behaviour surprising rather than merely noisy. The
folder map was keyed by the prefix, so two folders producing one prefix (a realm and a group with
the same name) shared an `existing` set and the first folder's directory — a stub could be written
into the wrong group or not at all; it is keyed by the folder now. A generated name is recorded as
taken, so a second API-bearing layer or a reload cannot write the stub over what the developer has
since put in the file. And a filled placeholder is forgotten, which the old code did not do: it kept
every claimed file in the set and rewrote the same stub on the next pass, over the developer's code.

What is still open is architectural and is recorded as a todo: the pass is a hostage of load order,
since a scan may run after the definition it should serve; generation writes into the source tree in
every intent, including the ones that only serve or write manifests; and `blong-kukum` now scaffolds
the same handlers on demand, which is the shape this feature should probably take.

### D-179 — Creator access to a guarded record - decided (b), adapt the specs

> _2026-09-16 · core/blong-gogo · superseded_

ANSWERED by the user (option b): adapt the specs, keep the enforcement unchanged. Done: the
organization spec now skips create (skipCreate) and edits the seeded organization the signed-in
admin is scoped to; the unit create spec passes unchanged (a unit created without an organization is
unscoped and therefore visible); the portal person-browse spec filters before waiting for the table.
Creator auto-grant (option a) was NOT chosen, so a newly created organization remains invisible to
its creator until a grant names it - the UI New form for party.organization therefore cannot
complete, which is documented in the spec header. Revisit (a) if organization creation must work
through the UI.

Superseded by `D-181`.

Superseded: the user chose the wildcard grant instead of adapting the specs, so the organization
create test and its baselines are restored (party Playwright 16 passed, 0 skipped).

### D-240 — A hop's leg id is dotted even when the wire method is slash-routed

> _2026-09-21 · core/blong-gogo · superseded_

The dispatch hop declares its leg with legName(forwarded) - the wire method with its separator as a
dot - while the forwarded $meta.method keeps the slash. Slash routing is a transport convention the
receiver strips (methodPath), and the leg grammar flattens a '/' to '-': declaring the slash form
produced gateway.db-gateway.application.register, whose second segment names no participant and
whose target the arrow had to guess at. The dotted id reads as every other leg does,
`<caller>.<target>.<method>`, and the ledger reads the target off it.

Superseded: the hop declares the wire method itself, slash and all (a decision retired with the
semantic-log package), rather than a dotted form of it.

Superseded by `D-249`.

The slash is lawful in a leg id now that the id is the method; the caller is no longer part of it,
so there is nothing to flatten away.

### D-276 — Startup silence: visibility change or loader design change

> _2026-09-26 · core/blong-gogo · superseded_

The startup silence (about 9-10 s before the first log line, and the same load ahead of tap's
output) is pre-existing and has no small fix. Two directions were offered and neither is safe to
take without the user's call:

Making it visible — logging during the component and handler import phase — is a change to the load
pipeline, small but touching the path every start goes through.

Making it faster means loading less eagerly (lazy or parallel handler imports), which is a design
change in the loader with real risk, and the profile says the cost is filesystem latency on a large
number of sequential module operations, so nothing short of that will move it.

The measurements, and the fact that both delays match the stashed baseline, are in the friction
entry about this in the same memory file. Nothing further is being changed until that decision is
made.

The user chose: reclaim automatically and keep the existing directory, a 1s default margin
configurable through the log config, and timing on every operation that reports progress.

### D-440 — linkGatewayKeys is a value bridge between two config paths, not a key source

> _2026-10-07 · core/blong-gogo · superseded_

The gateway resolves the pair its configuration names and the rpc client reads its own from
remote.client, so nothing connected the two and the client resolved no keys at all in a released
process. The bridge is made of accessors because the gateway resolves at plugin registration and the
client reads lazily on the first call, and a configured pair now wins: the accessor is only defined
where the path is empty, and mle.ts writes the resolved material back to the path it read, so one
reader never holds a recipe while the other holds keys. The channel itself moved with D-441: the
pair travels as an rc document under the pod home rather than as two variables, which is why the
deployment does not have to know any framework variable name.

Superseded by `D-441`.

The channel decision was taken: the pair is an rc document a deployment mounts, so the bridge is
left to the generated-pair case only.

### D-535 — A gateway's local resolution is gateway.skipSocket, not remote.canSkipSocket

> _2026-10-12 · core/blong-gogo · superseded_

The resolver asked one setting, canSkipSocket, whether a call may be answered in the process rather
than through the transport, and a process that serves a gateway inherited whatever an adapter or an
integration run was configured with. Those are two different questions. remote.canSkipSocket answers
for a process with no gateway to go through — a browser, a CLI run, a worker — while a gateway that
fronts calls is the process that has to say it for itself. The setting is authored as
gateway.skipSocket, beside the gateway port, and the loader resolves it into
remote.gatewaySkipSocket, which is the slice the resolver reads: the same three shapes (a boolean or
a regular-expression source), over the same bridge the key pair already uses (resolveGatewayPair
writes remote.client the same way, into the raw config the components read). A module-level value
set by the loader was tried first, was rejected in review, and was wrong in fact as well: it never
reached the resolver, so the earlier cluster pass proved nothing about skipSocket. A serving process
that says nothing goes through the transport — the transport is where a request's capabilities are
added (the forwarded headers, the identity the codec resolves, the trace, the progress channel), so
a local answer drops them without failing, and a regression introduced by circumventing the remote
call would otherwise pass every development run and appear only after a release. A run that names
integration or playwright is the stated exception: it is testing a process in one place, where the
sim and mock namespaces answer through dispatch and a dial reaches nothing, which is why integration
already asks for the local answer — the kustomize suite hung at ready ports 1 of 4 without it. The
session check keeps its own rule, and it is not the mixing this split removes: GatewayCodec asks for
the caller's session from inside its verification and calls the transport sender directly, before
any resolution, so RpcClient.sender still answers identity.checkInternal in-process through
Remote.localMethod.

Superseded by `D-537`.

Superseded: the gateway.skipSocket setting and the derived remote.gatewaySkipSocket are gone. The
two questions live with the code that answers them — the codec's skipGateway for routing,
canSkipSocket for the local answer — and the session step now goes through the resolver, which is
what made the extra setting and its bridge unnecessary.
